### 2026-10-11 – I did about 30 minutes of research between my sessions on some common uses for PCBs and parts I could use, and decided I would make a gaming keyboard. By this, I mean that it would only have keys WASD

**3.03h**

I did about 30 minutes of research between my sessions on some common uses for PCBs and parts I could use, and decided I would make a gaming keyboard. By this, I mean that it would only have keys WASD, number keys, CTRL, c, and V. I'm also trying to make a mousepad connection so that it can allow a tablet or smartphone to act as a computer. To do this, I had to scrap my previous work and I replaced it with several pushbuttons (if there is a special footprint for keyboard keys I will try to implement them in the future) and I added an rPI pico as the brain. It uses a 12 pin connector to connect to the touchpad, because KiCAD doesn't have one and I haven't confirmed if I want to implement it yet. I also did the footprints and wiring rails for the PCB. (The additional hours is just the research time, the actual design time is all featured in the timelapse)

### 2026-10-11 – In this session, I decided that I would attempt to make my PCB keyboard also function as a dock. By this, I mean that it would have a MicroSD slot to act as an external storage adaptor since my Mac bo

**1.75h**

In this session, I decided that I would attempt to make my PCB keyboard also function as a dock. By this, I mean that it would have a MicroSD slot to act as an external storage adaptor since my Mac book only has a full sized SD card slot (I want it to be functional instead of just cool). I also added a USB A and USB C port (the USB A is power only) since one can never have too many USBs. The schematics weren't difficult to create, as I only had to add 3 components and used google to find out what each port needed. However, many of the newly needed ports on the rPI PICO (brain for my project) were blocked off by other wiring, so I decided to fully rewire it. I think it looks a lot cleaner and I'm glad I did, because it will be easier for me during PCB build week. Attached are the most final versions of the schematic and PCB design, as of posting this entry.

I spent a long time troubleshooting my code. Even though I installed it and did the thing it prompted in my terminal, any instances called relating to the Raspberry Pi Pico were appearing as undefined error in VS code. I spent about half an hour failing to fix it, so I just wrote the code out for now, checked with AI (double checked with an experienced friend because I don't trust AI) to make sure it would run properly (I'm a java guy, its my first time using C++) and I'll try to switch it to Arduino when I get to actually building.
